opus-5.5.text:
That decision really came down to what kind of impact I wanted to have and what kind of life I wanted to build.

When I was finishing my PhD at Stanford, there were certainly good options in industry in the U.S. Big tech companies were investing heavily in AI, and the pay and resources were very attractive. But I kept asking myself: ten years from now, what do I want to have built? A company job would have meant contributing to someone else's roadmap, often on a narrow piece of a very large system. That can be valuable, but it wasn't what excited me most.

What excited me was the chance to build something from the ground up, a research direction, a lab, a group of young people who could grow into the next generation of leaders in the field. A university like Peking University gives you that. You have academic freedom, you can choose problems that may not pay off for five or ten years, and you work with some of the most talented students in China. Many of them are extremely hungry and capable. Being able to shape how they think about research is a kind of leverage you don't really get in a company.

Timing also mattered. I work on embodied intelligence: robots that can perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. I felt China was at an inflection point here. There's a very strong manufacturing and hardware supply chain, a huge range of real-world scenarios, and a lot of national and industry interest in robotics. For embodied AI, being close to hardware and real applications really matters. So returning didn't feel like stepping away from the frontier. It felt like moving toward where a lot of the action was going to be.

There was a personal side too. I grew up in China, and I always had a sense that if I could contribute something meaningful, I'd like it to be here. Coming back to Peking University let me combine that sense of belonging with a professional opportunity that felt unusually open.

Looking back, I think it was the right choice. Being in academia also didn't stop me from engaging with industry. In some ways it gave me a better foundation for that later, because I'd already built the research base and the team.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts building and leading a research group at Peking University with contributing to a company’s roadmap, but it does not identify Google as the company.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came down to the kind of problem I wanted to spend my life on. In industry, you're usually handed a product and a timeline, and the question is already decided for you. What I cared about was the question itself: how does a robot actually understand the physical world well enough to act in it? That's not something you solve in a quarter.

Peking University gave me something I couldn't get anywhere else, which was freedom and students. I could pick a direction that might take ten years, like embodied intelligence, and build a group of people who grow with the problem. Watching a student go from not knowing what a point cloud is to publishing work that changes how others think about manipulation, that's a very different kind of return on time.

There was also a personal piece. I'd done my PhD at Stanford and spent years in that environment, and I saw how strong the talent in China was becoming, but how much of the fundamental research ecosystem still needed people to come back and build it. Beijing is also where the robotics hardware is, where the manufacturing is, where you can walk to a factory and talk to the people who actually build the arms. For embodied AI, that proximity matters.

And frankly, a company job in the US would have been comfortable, but it felt like I'd be optimizing someone else's roadmap. I wanted to be in a position where, if I was wrong, it was my own bet that was wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says he wanted freedom to build a research group at Peking University instead of optimizing a US company’s roadmap, but it does not identify Google or frame the alternative as being a cog there.

astra-6.text: For me, the main appeal was the opportunity to pursue my own research questions and work with students. A company job in the United States could have been very attractive, but I felt an academic environment would give me more freedom to think about problems over the long term. Returning to Peking University was a chance to build something around those interests. It was less about choosing between two countries and more about choosing the kind of work I wanted to do.
